about: A fix to a command-line tool that turns titles into URL slugs: before removing every character outside a-z and 0-9, the code first splits each accented letter into the plain letter and its accent mark, so "Café" gives "cafe" instead of "caf".
reason: Approved second [of the 2 fixes approved in this step], with the design correction both reviewers [of the proposal] made: after NFKD [Unicode decomposition, which splits an accented letter into the plain letter and a combining accent mark], drop only the combining marks, so ß, ø and ł [letters with no such split] still become a hyphen as today. It closes 1 severity-3 finding [an observed defect, on a scale from 1, costs little, to 3, makes the result unusable: accented letters were dropped whole] and lifts the test case with titles "Café", "Crème Brûlée" and "HELLO World" from 0.3 to 1.0 [its grade, on a scale from 0 to 1]. The 2 classes of changed output, accented letters and compatibility forms [characters such as the ligature "ﬁ" that decompose to plain letters], both move to what the tool's specification already promises.

pattern.context: A program reduces text to an allowlist of plain characters, such as a-z and 0-9, by removing or replacing everything else, and its specification promises that accented letters keep their base letter.
pattern.problem: The filter treats an accented letter as one foreign character and drops it whole, so "Café" loses its last letter. Folding accents by a blanket rule risks changing letters that have no plain form.
pattern.solution: Before filtering, apply NFKD decomposition and drop only the combining marks it produces. Letters with no decomposition, such as ß, ø and ł, pass to the filter unchanged and are handled as before.
pattern.consequences: Accented letters and compatibility forms such as the ligature "ﬁ" now yield their plain letters, as the specification promises. Output for letters with no decomposition stays the same.
